subject: research/robofab-bootstrap

(2) Smallest self-assembling scale from 32 s - 2 t >= 30 s on the 0.25 grid for t=1,2,3,4,6 gives 1,2,3,4,6, matching section 2. (3) All ten chains for w0=24,60,100,130,140 under max and min policy re-derived by hand-written loop (e.g. 100 -> 3.0,2.5,2.0,1.5,1.0,None; 130 -> 4.0 repeating; 140 -> 4.5 repeating; min policy -> 1.0 then None) and all match section 4. (4) Stroke sets: stroke 160 gives scales 4.0,4.5,5.0 (5.0: 150 <= min(152,160); 5.5 needs 165 > 160) and 120 gives only 4.0, matching section 3. evidence.craft: Read src/robofab_bootstrap/model.py (223 lines), tests/test_bootstrap.py, experiments/run.py, figure.py, pyproject.toml. Defects: (a) the geometry engine is a copy of robofab-selfparts/model.py, so two engines can drift (declared in the docstring, but a shared package would be the senior choice); (b) ARMS_ALL is defined at module line 147, after Model.moves uses it at line 96 (works only because it is resolved at call time); the 'free' arm and `gravity` toggle are unused here; (c) chain()'s third policy branch (line 221, nearest-opening) is dead/untested and an unknown policy string silently falls through to it; (d) min_jaw re-runs a full subset DP ~11 bisection times per scale, uncached, and chain/run.py recompute it for the same scales: run.py takes 44 s versus the README's ~2 s; (e) min_jaw returns None for 'no order up to 260 mm' and chain() treats it as unbuildable without a message, a silent fallback; hi=260 mm is hard-coded though scale 7 needs 210 (fine) and larger scales would silently report None; (f) run.py imports Model, gripper, search without using them; (g) moves() uses `break` after the first feasible axis, so grasp axis is not reported meaningfully; (h) pad_t has no effect on assembly feasibility: min_jaw(1.0), min_jaw(2.0) were identical for pad_t=1..16 and for arms free/top/side, so pad geometry code is exercised but never binding. Code is otherwise compact, readable and deterministic with no dependencies.
evidence.claims: Checked each claim against files: 24 vs 30 mm, s >= t, 30 t <= stroke, chain lengths 3 and 5, fixed points 4.0 and 4.5, 'search confirms algebra rather than finding something new': all backed by experiments/results.txt and my recomputation, and the README is unusually frank that the headline is closed-form given an assumed opening. Limitations section is specific (no motors, tolerance, shrinkage, force, print size) and says simulation only; AI assistance disclosed; no marketing claims. Unbacked or wrong: README command comment 'PYTHONPATH=src python3 experiments/run.py  # ~2 s' is false (43.7 s measured), a 20x error; SVG title 'a gripper copies itself only above scale 4' is wrong at exactly scale 4.0, where the table says yes (should be 'from scale 4'); README says the opening 32 s - 2 t uses 'the 32 mm rail gap' but nothing in the code derives it from the geometry (the rails in gripper() give an inner gap 40-4-4 = 32, so it is consistent, but unchecked by a test). Citations (Zykov 2005 Nature 435:163, Jones 2011 Robotica 29:177, Tian 2024 ICRA) look right from memory, and the README admits they were not re-verified; whitepaper cites authors as 'others'. Live page not loaded.
evidence.fitness: For research use: nearest prior work is the kinematic self-replication and closure literature (Freitas and Merkle, Kinematic Self-Replicating Machines, 2004; Moses and Chirikjian, Robotic self-replication, Annu. Rev. Control Robot. Auton. Syst. 2020; RepRap, Jones 2011 which the README does cite) and assembly sequence planning by subset/AND-OR search (Homem de Mello and Sanderson 1991; Wilson and Latombe 1994), none of which the paper cites except RepRap. The result is not new in content: the 'exhaustive search' returns min_jaw = 30 s, which is just the narrow side of the widest part scaled by s (pad_t and approach direction do not change it, verified), and the headline s >= t follows from an assumed opening formula by one line of algebra, as the README concedes. Sound within its assumptions, but a researcher could not build on it: the opening model is not tied to a mechanism, isotropic scaling ignores that torque, mass and stiffness scale differently from length, the only non-scaling element is the pad, and there is one toy design. The bootstrapping chain as a graph of (scale, opening) is a clean framing, but a reader gets nothing the one-line inequality does not already give.
evidence.domain: Compared against the replication-closure framing of Freitas and Merkle and Moses and Chirikjian (what fraction of parts and capabilities a machine can make, vitamins versus replicable parts) and against assembly-planning practice (precedence/AND-OR graphs, grasp planning with force closure). Departures a senior reviewer would flag: jaw opening is assumed, not computed from a linkage or actuator; the grasp test is bounding-box width versus opening, not force-closure; assembly feasibility is axis-aligned boxes with six removal directions; scaling is isotropic with fixed pads, so 'self-assembly starts at s = t' is a statement about two arbitrary constants; no replication ratio or closure metric is defined. The honest limitations section is what a reviewer would credit; the method itself would not be signed off as evidence about real grippers, and the paper would not clear a robotics venue as it stands.

defects.what: Headline chain results (policy 'max' and the stroke cap) are not asserted by any test: seeded mutations that make the policy pick the smallest scale (line 221) or ignore the stroke in chain() (line 222) leave all 6 tests green. test_chain_runs_with_big_seed checks only length and non-None; results.txt is never compared.

The exhaustive assembly search adds nothing to the headline: min_jaw equals 30 s (narrow side of the cover) for every scale, independent of pad_t and arm, and the self-assembly threshold s >= t follows from an assumed formula opening = 32 s - 2 t. The paper and README say this honestly, but the project therefore has no result a researcher can build on and omits the replication-closure and assembly-planning literature it sits in.
README claims experiments/run.py takes ~2 s; measured 43.7 s because min_jaw reruns the full subset DP (about 11 bisection calls) per scale and per call, uncached.
SVG title says a gripper copies itself 'only above scale 4' but the table (and the figure's own data) says it can at exactly 4.0.

Dead or silent code: ARMS_ALL defined after its first use; chain() falls through to an untested nearest-opening policy for any unknown policy string; min_jaw returns None for 'nothing up to 260 mm' with no message; run.py imports unused Model, gripper, search; geometry engine duplicated from robofab-selfparts.

verdict: Audited 2026-11-07 by running the code. Tests pass (6) and experiments/results.txt reproduces byte for byte (43.7 s, not the README's ~2 s). I recomputed table 1, the pad-thickness thresholds, the stroke-cap sets and all ten chains from a first-principles rule (need 30 s, opening 32 s - 2 t) without calling the search, and every number matches, so correctness and claims score 3 for the stated stylised model. It does not meet the bar: verification is 2 (6 of 8 seeded mutations caught; the two that changed the chain policy and the stroke cap passed all tests), and fitness and domain are 1 because the result is the algebra of an assumed formula, the search is vacuous for the headline (min_jaw is just 30 s, unaffected by pad thickness or arm), and the paper does not cite or compare to the self-replication closure or assembly-planning literature. The README's candour about all this is its main strength. Finished (completeness 3) but not at the level of a senior practitioner. Median 2. Suggested small fixes: add tests that pin the chain strings for w0=100 and 130 under both policies and a stroke-capped chain, correct the ~2 s claim, and fix the SVG title.
